name: Parkinson's Disease
summary: Large-amplitude movement, cueing, strength, balance, gait and aerobic exercise help preserve function and manage bradykinesia and falls risk.

firstSteps: Assess gait speed, turning, freezing triggers, balance, falls and dual-task difficulty.
Teach one amplitude strategy and one cueing strategy.

stages.label: Start: assess and set up
stages.goal: Target bradykinesia, gait, balance, freezing and deconditioning with large-amplitude and task-specific practice.
do: Assess gait speed, turning, freezing triggers, balance, falls and dual-task difficulty.
Teach one amplitude strategy and one cueing strategy.
Assess: Gait speed, freezing and turning
moveOn: Baseline recorded: Timed Up and Go

stages.label: Treat: build capacity
stages.goal: Consider medication on/off periods when scheduling challenging mobility work.
when: Baseline recorded: Timed Up and Go
dose: Large-amplitude movement: 1–2 sets × 8–10 repetitions of major patterns.
Balance/reactive stepping: 10–20 minutes, 3+ days/week as safe.
Aerobic exercise: build toward 20–30 minutes on most days.
Gait cueing: short focused bouts using visual or auditory cues.
moveOn: Increase amplitude, complexity and dual-task demand
Train turning, community mobility and floor transfers

stages.label: Progress and self-manage
stages.goal: Build lifelong exercise habits because the condition is progressive.
when: Increase amplitude, complexity and dual-task demand
Train turning, community mobility and floor transfers
dose: Increase amplitude, speed, turning challenge and dual-task demand.
Progress from predictable clinic tasks to community mobility.

manual: Gentle mobility techniques for secondary musculoskeletal stiffness
Manual therapy should not replace active amplitude and gait training
Manual therapy can address secondary musculoskeletal stiffness but should not be the main Parkinson's intervention.
Use it only if it makes active movement practice easier.
modalities: External visual/auditory cueing can improve gait in selected patients
Passive electrotherapy is not a core intervention
External cueing is often more clinically useful than passive electrotherapy.
progression: Increase amplitude, complexity and dual-task demand
Train turning, community mobility and floor transfers

Progress from predictable clinic tasks to community mobility.
education: Encourage regular vigorous-enough exercise when medically safe.
Discuss falls prevention and home setup.
escalation: Medical review for falls, medication-related fluctuations, syncope or rapid functional change
